extension.value: An e-visa CANNOT be extended or renewed from inside Vietnam. travel.state.gov: 'Vietnam does not allow you to renew or extend an E-visa while you are in the country.' It also notes Vietnam 'usually only gives you a visa for the exact time period you requested' — so the 90-day ceiling is not a default grant, and asking for too little cannot be fixed later. Separately, holders of other visa types seeking an extension or resolving an overstay must appear IN PERSON at the Immigration Office for the jurisdiction where they are staying: Hanoi, 69 Mac Thai To St, Yen Hoa Ward (024 3825-7941); Da Nang, 78 Le Loi, Hai Chau (central Vietnam); HCMC, 196 Nguyen Thi Minh Khai, Xuan Hoa Ward (028 3829-9398).

evisa_traps.value: Four ways an e-visa fails at the border, all from travel.state.gov. (1) PORT MISMATCH: 'The entry and exit location must match the port of entry you chose when you applied' — an e-visa naming Noi Bai does not work if you land at Tan Son Nhat. (2) ERRORS: if the e-visa has a mistake, 'immigration may not let you enter the country. You may have to pay a travel agency at the airport for an expensive visa sponsorship.' (3) PRINT IT: 'You must print your E-visa and bring it with your valid passport' — a phone screen is not stated as sufficient. (4) NO RESCUE: 'The U.S. embassy and consulate general cannot change your E-visa information or speed up your application.'
evisa_traps.notes: This is the spine of vietnam-evisa-how-to-apply and a genuine swamp: four independent, pre-departure, self-inflicted failure modes with an expensive airport remedy. Neither panel model surfaced any of the four. CLOSED the 'is printing really enforced' question editorially rather than by evidence: the official instruction is unambiguous ('You must print your E-visa'), the practice is not documentable from any source, and the cost of complying is one sheet of paper. Write 'print it' without hedging; do not speculate about enforcement.

Six months beyond the date of arrival, plus at least one blank page per entry stamp. Separately, and less widely known: an e-visa's validity must be at least 30 days SHORTER than the passport's remaining validity.
record.notes: The second half is from evisa.gov.vn's FAQ (https://evisa.gov.vn/faq), read 2026-10-12, verbatim: 'the validity of the electronic visa must be at least 30 days shorter than the passport validity.' This compounds with the 6-month rule and is the genuinely non-obvious part: a traveler whose passport expires in just over 6 months clears the entry rule but CANNOT be granted a 90-day e-visa — the system will cap or refuse it. No secondary source I checked states this. Strong candidate for a fact span. CONTRADICTION CONFIRMED 2026-10-12: travel.state.gov contradicts ITSELF on blank pages — its entry-requirements block says 'You must have 1 blank page available per stamp', while its E-visa warnings block says 'Your passport must have at least 2 blank pages required for stamps.' ChatGPT flagged exactly this internal conflict and was right; I had recorded only the 1-page figure. Write the conservative number (2+) and do not cite the page as if it spoke with one voice.

Safe practice: ensure passport is valid for at least 6 months beyond intended stay.

Visitors are required to register their temporary residence with the local police station where they are staying overnight. Hotels typically handle this for registered guests; private stays (Airbnb, homestays) may require the host or guest to register. The U.S. Embassy notes this requirement applies to all visitors including Vietnamese. Airport authorities and airlines routinely check passports even for domestic flights. Children exiting Vietnam may require a Vietnamese passport or exit visa if they have Vietnamese parentage — contact the nearest Vietnamese immigration office.

police_registration.value: Every visitor must register their overnight address with the local police — this applies to everyone staying in Vietnam, Vietnamese citizens included. Hotels do it automatically from your passport at check-in, which is why they ask for it. The gap is informal stays: an Airbnb, a homestay or a friend's apartment, where the host is responsible and may not do it.

record.value: Not obligatory in Vietnam. Tipping is appreciated but not expected in most local establishments. atm_fees.value: The durable fact is the STRUCTURE, not the number: Vietnamese ATMs charge a FLAT fee per withdrawal, not a percentage, and they cap each withdrawal low. So the cost per dollar is set by how much you take out at once. A 55,000 VND fee on a 2,000,000 VND withdrawal (~$75) is about 2.7%; the same fee on a 10,000,000 VND withdrawal (~$380) is about 0.55%. The rule that follows holds whatever the exact figures: find a bank with a high per-transaction cap and withdraw the maximum, rarely — never small amounts, often. Your US bank's own foreign-transaction fee stacks on top of this.

record.value: Vietnam Railways operates the Reunification Express (Bắc–Nam) between Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City, ~1,726 km, taking roughly 32–36 hours depending on service. record.value: Driving is on the right side. US-issued International Driving Permits (IDPs) are NOT recognized in Vietnam because the US is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention, while Vietnam recognizes only 1968 Vienna Convention IDPs. A US license alone is not valid for driving in Vietnam. Self-driving is strongly discouraged for short-term visitors due to traffic conditions, insurance complications, and the IDP issue. Most travelers hire a car with driver or use ride-sharing.
record.notes: Sources indicate Vietnam requires a 1968 Vienna Convention IDP. The US issues IDPs under the 1949 Convention. This is a significant practical barrier. Blood alcohol limit: Vietnam has a zero-tolerance policy for alcohol while driving (BAC 0.00). Fines for violations are steep. Verify current enforcement and any changes with the Vietnamese Embassy or a reputable car rental agency before considering self-drive.

record.value: Hanoi: cool or cold and misty December–March; hot, humid and rainy June–August. Hue: wetter September–February. Hoi An: wetter September–January. Ho Chi Minh City and Mekong Delta: rainy May–November, generally drier December–April. These are seasonal patterns, not forecasts.

Vietnam is ~1,000 miles north-to-south and has no single season — this is the defining planning fact. THREE regimes: (1) NORTH (Hanoi, Sapa, Ha Long, Ninh Binh) has four seasons including a genuinely cold, damp winter (Dec-Feb, 50s-60s F, grey drizzle 'mua phun'), a hot humid summer (Jun-Aug, 90s F, heaviest rain) and short pleasant shoulders (Oct-Nov, Mar-Apr). (2) CENTRE (Hue, Da Nang, Hoi An) is driest Feb-Aug and has a short, violent wet season Sep-Nov — typhoon season, and Hoi An floods most years. (3) SOUTH (HCMC, Mekong, Phu Quoc) is tropical and warm year-round, split into dry (Dec-Apr) and wet (May-Nov, afternoon downpours rather than all-day rain).
record.notes: The consequence no single-answer article can state: there is NO month that is good everywhere. Oct-Nov is excellent in the north and the worst of the year in the centre; Jun-Aug is good for the centre's beaches and brutal in Hanoi. This is a genuine swamp — an itinerary's shape is decided by it.

record.value: Vietnam spans multiple climate zones. Central (Hue, Da Nang, Hoi An): transitional — dry hot season Feb–Aug; typhoon/rainy season Sep–Dec. South (HCMC, Mekong Delta): tropical — hot year-round (75–95°F); distinct wet season May–Nov and dry season Dec–Apr. Central Highlands (Da Lat): cooler year-round, sweater weather at night. Phu Quoc: tropical; dry season Nov–Apr, wet season May–Oct.

Petty theft, overwhelmingly. State Dept, read 2026-10-12, verbatim: 'Vietnam is generally a safe destination for travelers. Petty crime is common, especially in popular tourist locations.' The dominant specific mode is drive-by phone and bag snatching from a moving motorbike, in Ho Chi Minh City above all. Violent crime against foreigners is rare. The genuinely under-weighted risk is ROAD TRAFFIC: motorbike injury is the leading cause of serious harm and medical evacuation for visitors, not crime.
record.notes: The risk an American fears (crime, residual war hostility) and the risk that actually hurts them (traffic) are different risks. The safety article should say so in the first paragraph.

record.value: CDC recommends keeping routine vaccinations current, hepatitis A for eligible unvaccinated travelers and hepatitis B for unvaccinated travelers of all ages. Japanese encephalitis vaccination depends on duration, rural exposure and activities. Malaria prevention is itinerary-specific: CDC lists no transmission in Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City, Da Nang, Hai Phong, Nha Trang or Quy Nhon, but identifies rural risk areas. Two different claims, and the article is the distinction. REQUIRED FOR ENTRY: none — the State Department says 'No vaccinations are required.' RECOMMENDED by CDC for Vietnam: Hepatitis A (unvaccinated travellers 1 year and older), Hepatitis B (unvaccinated travellers of all ages), Typhoid ('recommended for most travelers'), plus routine vaccines up to date and COVID-19. Conditional, not blanket: Japanese encephalitis (only for long stays or rural living), Rabies (dog exposure risk), Measles, Monkeypox (activity-based). Nothing is required at the border; all of it is a conversation with a travel clinic ideally a month out.

value: Taxi scams
Taxi meter manipulation and lookalike liveries — the reason Grab/Xanh SM is the standing advice: the fare is fixed before the ride and there is no meter to argue with.
The 500,000 / 20,000 dong note confusion at change — similar colours, a 25x difference. Learn the two notes before arriving.
Cyclo and xich lo rides where the agreed price turns out to be per person, per hour, or in USD.
Shoe-repair and fruit-basket approaches in Hanoi's Old Quarter: an unsolicited service performed before a price is named, then an aggressive price.
Motorbike rental damage claims — pre-existing scratches charged at return. Photograph the whole bike, with the renter present, before riding off.
'Closed today' redirection at major sights, steering to a commission shop or alternate tour.

malaria.value: Mostly NOT a concern on a standard tourist itinerary, which contradicts the generic 'take antimalarials for Southeast Asia' advice. CDC, verbatim: transmission is in 'Rural areas only; rare cases in the Mekong and Red River Deltas', and there is 'None in the cities of Da Nang, Hai Phong, Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City (Saigon), Nha Trang, and Quy Nhon.' So a Hanoi / Ha Long / Hoi An / HCMC trip has essentially no malaria exposure. Chemoprophylaxis is recommended for rural transmission areas, with named provinces including Binh Phuoc, Dak Lak, Dak Nong, Gia Lai, Khanh Hoa, Kon Tum, Lam Dong, Ninh Thuan and Tay Ninh. Chloroquine and mefloquine resistance is present, so those two are not the drugs.
malaria.notes: Strong candidate for a fact span and a genuinely money-saving finding: most readers are told to buy antimalarials they do not need. CARE REQUIRED on two points before writing: (1) Lam Dong is Da Lat's province and appears on the province list, so do not write 'Da Lat is risk-free' — CDC names provinces for DRUG CHOICE within transmission areas, which is not the same as saying the whole province transmits. (2) Sapa and Ha Giang are rural northern areas and are therefore NOT covered by the city exemption. Mosquito-bite avoidance still applies everywhere for dengue, which has no vaccine in this context.

record.value: Excellent and cheap. Viettel (widest rural coverage, state-owned), Vinaphone and Mobifone are the three carriers; Viettel is the default choice for anyone going to Sapa, Ha Giang or the Mekong. Physical tourist SIMs are sold at airport arrivals and require passport registration. eSIM is supported by all three and by the usual resellers (Airalo and similar), which is the lower-friction route for a recent iPhone — installed before departure, live on landing.

record.value: Local SIM cards (physical and eSIM) widely available and affordable. Major carriers: Viettel (largest, best rural coverage), Vinaphone, MobiFone. Tourist SIMs with data packages available at airports, carrier stores, and authorized agents. eSIMs from international providers (Airalo, Holafly, Nomad, etc.) work and connect to Viettel/Vinaphone/MobiFone networks. 4G is near-universal including on most of the Ha Giang loop and in Sapa; 5G is live in Hanoi, HCMC and Da Nang. Dead zones are limited to deep karst valleys, parts of Ha Long Bay out on the water, and remote trekking. Wi-Fi is free and ubiquitous in cafes, hotels and many restaurants — more reliably so than in the US.

Train: Da Nang railway station, then taxi/Grab to Hoi An (~45 min). Reunification Express stops at Da Nang. Bus: local buses and tourist shuttles from Da Nang, Hue (~3–4 hours by road over Hai Van Pass).
Bicycle, on foot, and Grab for the beach. The Ancient Town is pedestrianised for much of the day. An Bang and Cua Dai beaches are 10-15 minutes by bike.
